Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: Six workers paint a hall in ten days. All the workers work at the same rate. How many days would four workers need to paint the same hall?
Before any calculation, let's ask, more days or fewer? Fewer workers paint the same hall. So less gets done each day, and the job takes longer. So it takes more than ten days.
at: So it takes more than ten days

slides.say: So choice number one, six and two thirds, and choice number four, eight, are out. Both are less than ten days.

Careful, this is the trap of this question. With the ratio table, we'd multiply four times ten, divide by six, and get six and two thirds. That's fewer days with fewer workers, which makes no sense. That calculation assumes the same days per worker in both rows. But fewer workers need more days for the same job. We need the total work to stay the same instead.
at: and get six and two thirds

slides: We'll solve it two ways, the math way with the whole job, and then by understanding, with one worker.

slides.say: Let's start with the math way. It's the same hall, so the whole job stays the same. We measure it in worker-days. One worker-day is one worker working for one day.
at: the whole job stays the same

slides.say: Six workers for ten days. Six times ten is sixty worker-days. That's the whole hall.
Now four workers do the same sixty worker-days. So four times the number of days is sixty. The days are sixty divided by four, fifteen.
at: So four times the number of days

slides.say: Fifteen is more than ten, just as we expected. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Why not twelve, choice number two? Twelve comes from two fewer workers, so two more days. But workers and days don't change by the same amount. Four workers for twelve days is only forty-eight worker-days, not sixty. Out.

[pause] Now by understanding. We start again from the givens. Six workers paint the hall in ten days. How long would one worker need alone? Six times as long, because he does the work of six people by himself. Ten times six is sixty days.
at: Ten times six is sixty days

slides.say: Now four workers. Four people share the job, so it takes a quarter of the time of one worker. Sixty divided by four is fifteen days.
at: Sixty divided by four is fifteen

slides.say: So here's the rule for the same job at the same rate. The number of workers times the days stays the same. This is called inverse proportion. One quantity doubles, and the other halves. Workers and days on the same job. Speed and time on the same road. People and the days a food supply lasts.
at: times the days stays the same

slides.say: Let's see it once more. Eight hikers have food for six days. How long does the same food last for twelve hikers? Eight times six is forty-eight hiker-days. Forty-eight divided by twelve is four days. More hikers, fewer days.
So before you build a ratio table, ask yourself, when one grows, does the other grow too, or does it shrink? Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
